newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade bourse weekly turnover sharply down.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade bourse weekly turnover sharply down.

text.p: The Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE) on Monday reported a plunge of almost 32 percent in its turnover during the week ending October 4 -- a fall traders attributed to tight market liquidity.
Total weekly turnover dropped to 25.39 million dinars ($5.027 million) in 156 transactions, from 37.93 million dinars in 185 deals a week ago, the bourse said.
Market liquidity began to deteriorate when the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) introduced a 10 percent reserve requirement in mid-September.
Since then, commercial banks have set aside almost 270 million dinars for the reserve requirement, a central bank official told Reuters.
Traders said overall liquidity was bad but slightly improved from a week ago. But the quality of issuers deteriorated and demand for securities remained low.
Market participants normally withdraw funds to pay salaries and pensions in the first week of the month, and this also put the brakes on otherwise slack market activity, a trader said.

Despite the sluggish market, the commercial paper segment bucked the trend with a lively start to the month. Those securities dominated the bourse activity with 137 deals worth 22.49 million dinars, up from 18.87 million dinars the previous week.
Treasury bills were traded 14 times for a volume of 2.302 million dinars.
Interest rates both on commercial paper and treasury bills ranged between 44 and 644 percent per annum.
"Last week saw a slight increase in the daily interest rates on commercial paper and treasury bills to 0.5 percent from 0.45 percent," a trader said.
There was no trade in the NBY short-term bonds, normally the most attractive paper.

The bourse reported only one deal in wheat selling forward contracts worth 109,000 dinars. But traders were optimistic that the investor interest in the contracts would increase as their December 3 sale-date approaches.
"Investors now try to calculate what is in it for them, to analyse all pros and cons, but they have plenty of time anyway," a market analyst said.
